chapters.title: The Making of the Heavens and the Earth
chapters.html:
Genesis 1

1In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.

2And the earth was wild and waste, and darkness lay over the face of the deep, and the breath of God was hovering over the face of the waters.

3And God said, "Light — be." And light was.

4And God saw the light, that it was good; and God made a division between the light and the darkness.

5And God called the light Day, and the darkness He called Night. And it was evening, and it was morning — day one.

The Second Day

6And God said, "Let there be a beaten expanse in the midst of the waters, and let it divide between waters and waters."

7And God made the expanse, and He divided between the waters that were beneath the expanse and the waters that were above the expanse. And it was so.

8And God called the expanse Heaven. And it was evening, and it was morning — a second day.

The Third Day

9And God said, "Let the waters beneath the heavens be gathered to one place, and let the dry ground be seen." And it was so.

10And God called the dry ground Earth, and the gathering of the waters He called Seas. And God saw that it was good.

11And God said, "Let the earth grow green with growing things: seed-bearing plants, and fruit trees making fruit after their kind, with their seed in them, upon the earth." And it was so.

12And the earth brought out growing things — seed-bearing plants after their kind, and trees making fruit with their seed in them after their kind. And God saw that it was good.

13And it was evening, and it was morning — a third day.

The Fourth Day

14And God said, "Let there be lamps in the expanse of the heavens, to divide between the day and the night; and let them be for signs, and for appointed times, and for days and years.

15And let them be lamps in the expanse of the heavens, to give light upon the earth." And it was so.

16And God made the two great lamps — the greater lamp for the rule of the day, and the lesser lamp for the rule of the night — and the stars.

17And God set them in the expanse of the heavens, to give light upon the earth,

18and to rule over the day and over the night, and to divide between the light and the darkness. And God saw that it was good.

19And it was evening, and it was morning — a fourth day.

The Fifth Day

20And God said, "Let the waters swarm with swarms of living souls, and let birds fly above the earth, across the face of the expanse of the heavens."

21And God created the great sea-monsters, and every living soul that creeps, with which the waters swarmed, after their kind, and every winged bird after its kind. And God saw that it was good.

22And God blessed them, saying, "Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas; and let the birds multiply in the earth."

23And it was evening, and it was morning — a fifth day.

The Sixth Day

24And God said, "Let the earth bring out living souls after their kind — cattle, and creeping things, and the living things of the earth after their kind." And it was so.

25And God made the living things of the earth after their kind, and the cattle after their kind, and everything that creeps on the ground after its kind. And God saw that it was good.

26And God said, "Let us make humankind in our image, according to our likeness; and let them hold sway over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the heavens, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth."

27And God created the human in His image;
in the image of God He created him;
male and female He created them.

28And God blessed them, and God said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and take it under foot; and hold sway over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the heavens, and over every living thing that creeps upon the earth."

29And God said, "Look — I have given you every seed-bearing plant that is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree that has in it tree-fruit bearing seed. To you it shall be for food.

30And to every living thing of the earth, and to every bird of the heavens, and to everything that creeps upon the earth, everything with a living soul in it — every green plant for food." And it was so.

31And God saw everything that He had made, and look — it was very good. And it was evening, and it was morning — the sixth day.

Notes

  • v1 "In the beginning" — Heb. bereshit. The word is grammatically a construct form, which is why some read the opening as one long sentence: "When God began to create the heavens and the earth — the earth being wild and waste — God said, 'Light, be.'" That reading makes v1 a subordinate clause rather than a standing declaration. The traditional absolute reading is kept here because Hebrew does permit it and because the sentence carries its own weight, but the reader should know the first three words of the Bible are contested.
  • v1 "created" — Heb. bara. Across the whole Hebrew Bible this verb never takes a human subject. It is reserved for God. English "create" is worn down by ordinary use in a way the Hebrew word is not.
  • v1 "the heavens and the earth" — a merism: naming the two poles to mean everything between them, the way we say "searched high and low." Not two items on a list.
  • v2 "wild and waste" — Heb. tohu wa-vohu, a rhyming jingle. "Formless and void" is accurate but sounds like philosophy; the Hebrew sounds like a phrase, almost a taunt. It describes a desert waste — uninhabitable, not empty of matter.
  • v2 "the breath of God was hovering" — Heb. ruach is wind, breath, and spirit in one word, and no English choice keeps all three. Merachefet (hovering) is rare; Deuteronomy 32:11 uses it of an eagle fluttering over its nest. The image is a bird brooding over the water, not a ghost drifting.
  • v3 "Light — be." And light was. — Heb. yehi 'or wa-yehi 'or. Two words, then the same two words with a single letter added — a prefixed vav, the Hebrew "and." The command itself is three syllables. Any English longer than that is already a commentary.
  • v4 "it was good" — Heb. tov. Closer to "it worked," "it was fit for what it was for." A good knife is tov. The moral sense we hear in English "good" is present in Hebrew elsewhere but is not what is being said about light.
  • v5 "day one" — Heb. yom echad, a cardinal number, not the ordinal "first." Days two through six then take ordinals. Almost every English Bible flattens this to "the first day," losing a deliberate oddity: before there is a second day, there is no first — there is only one. The pattern is worth watching to the end of the chapter: day one is a cardinal, days two through five are bare ordinals with no article, and the sixth alone is yom ha-shishi, the sixth day. Only the last one gets a definite article.
  • v6 "beaten expanse" — Heb. raqia, from the root raqa. Everywhere that verb appears it means making something flat and broad by beating or pressure: gold hammered into plates and cut into threads (Exod 39:3), bronze censers beaten into a plating for the altar (Num 17:4), a goldsmith overlaying an idol (Isa 40:19), beaten silver from Tarshish (Jer 10:9) — and also the earth spread out over the waters (Ps 136:6, Isa 42:5), and a foot stamping the ground (Ezek 6:11, 2 Sam 22:43).

What the root does not say is dome. Beating and stamping make things flat, not curved, and when Ezekiel sees a raqia (1:22) the verb he uses is natui, stretched out, the word for pitching a tent. So the familiar English options are four different interpretations rather than four synonyms: "firmament" comes from Latin firmamentum, rendering Greek stereoma, "a solid thing" — the Septuagint translators had already decided it was solid; "vault" and "dome" supply a curve the Hebrew never mentions; "expanse" keeps the spreading and drops the beating. Only the process is certain: something thin and broad, made by being beaten or stretched out.

Solidity is argued from elsewhere, and the arguments are from the text rather than the root: Job 37:18 asks whether you can spread out the skies hard as a cast mirror, and Ezekiel 1:26 sets a throne on top of one. - v14 "appointed times" — Heb. mo'adim, the standard word for the festival calendar. The lamps are not decoration and not merely clocks; they are hung to tell Israel when to gather. - v16 "the two great lamps" — the sun and the moon are never named in this chapter, though Hebrew has ordinary words for both. Every neighbouring culture worshipped them under those names. Here they are demoted to fixtures, hung up like lamps in a room, and the stars get two words tacked onto the end of a sentence. - v26 "Let us make" — Heb. na'aseh, first person plural. The Hebrew simply says it, and any explanation offered for it — a heavenly court, a plural of deliberation, a plural of majesty — is the reader's, not the text's. - v26, 28 "hold sway," "take it under foot" — Heb. radah and kavash. Both are hard words. Radah is what a king does to subjects; kavash is used of subduing conquered land and of forcing a person down. "Have dominion" and "subdue" are not softenings, but four centuries of use have made them sound ceremonial. They are not. - v27 — the prose breaks into three balanced lines here and nowhere else in the chapter. Set as poetry because the Hebrew is. - vv20, 21, 24, 30 "living soul" — Heb. nephesh chayyah. The King James renders this phrase "living creature" every time it belongs to an animal, and "living soul" in 2:7 when God breathes into the human. It is the same two Hebrew words. The split is the translator's, not the text's, and most modern English Bibles have kept the habit. Rendered identically here, because the Hebrew is identical. - v30 "everything with a living soul in it" — Heb. asher bo nephesh chayyah, "in which there is a living soul." The bo ("in it") is masculine; eretz, earth, is feminine, as the feminine verb hayetah in v2 shows. So the clause cannot reach back to the earth — grammar rules it out. The soul is in the creeping thing, not in the ground it crawls on. English word order makes this ambiguous where Hebrew is not, which is why the clause is moved here. - "soul" — nephesh is not the Greek immortal soul. The root sense is throat: the neck, where breath and food pass. From there it means breath, appetite, hunger, life, and finally the self. A nephesh chayyah is a breathing, hungry, living thing — which is why this verse, having listed everything with a throat, goes on to say what they may eat. - v31 "very good" — Heb. tov me'od. The only time the verdict is intensified, and it is passed on the whole, not on the last item made.

chapters.title: The Garden, and the Forming of the Human
chapters.html:
Genesis 2

1And the heavens and the earth were finished, and all their array.

2And on the seventh day God finished the work that He had done, and He ceased on the seventh day from all the work that He had done.

3And God blessed the seventh day and set it apart, because on it He ceased from all His work, which God had created to make.

The Ground and the Man

4These are the begettings of the heavens and the earth when they were created, in the day that the LORD God made earth and heaven.

5No shrub of the field was yet in the earth, and no plant of the field had yet sprung up, for the LORD God had not sent rain upon the earth, and there was no human to serve the ground.

6But a flow would go up from the earth and water the whole face of the ground.

7And the LORD God shaped the human of dust from the ground, and blew into his nostrils the breath of lives, and the human became a living soul.

8And the LORD God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, and there He put the human whom He had shaped.

9And the LORD God made grow from the ground every tree desirable to look at and good for food, and the tree of life in the middle of the garden, and the tree of the knowing of good and evil.

10And a river goes out from Eden to water the garden, and from there it divides and becomes four heads.

11The name of the first is Pishon; it is the one winding through all the land of Havilah, where there is gold.

12And the gold of that land is good; bdellium is there, and the onyx stone.

13And the name of the second river is Gihon; it is the one winding through all the land of Cush.

14And the name of the third river is Tigris; it is the one going east of Asshur. And the fourth river is the Euphrates.

15And the LORD God took the human and set him down in the garden of Eden, to serve it and to keep it.

16And the LORD God laid a charge upon the human, saying, "From every tree of the garden you may surely eat.

17But from the tree of the knowing of good and evil you shall not eat, for on the day you eat from it, dying you shall die."

The One Facing Him

18And the LORD God said, "It is not good for the human to be alone. I will make for him a help as his counterpart."

19And the LORD God shaped from the ground every living thing of the field and every bird of the heavens, and brought them to the human to see what he would call them; and whatever the human called each living soul, that was its name.

20And the human gave names to all the cattle, and to the birds of the heavens, and to every living thing of the field. But for the human he found no help as his counterpart.

21And the LORD God made a deep sleep fall upon the human, and he slept; and He took one of his sides and closed up the flesh in its place.

22And the LORD God built the side that He had taken from the human into a woman, and He brought her to the human.

23And the human said,
"This one, this time, is bone of my bones
and flesh of my flesh.
This one shall be called Woman,
for from Man was this one taken."

24Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother and clings to his woman, and they become one flesh.

25And the two of them were naked, the human and his woman, and they were not ashamed.

Notes

  • v4 "begettings" — Heb. toledot, the word that structures the whole book: these are the begettings of Noah, of Terah, of Isaac. It normally introduces a family line. Here it is applied to the sky and the ground, as though heaven and earth were parents with descendants. Notice also that the verse ends by reversing itself: it opens with the heavens and the earth and closes with earth and heaven. The order flips inside one verse, and the whole account that follows is told from the ground up.
  • v4 "the LORD God" — the divine name YHWH appears for the first time here, paired with Elohim. Chapter 1 used Elohim alone, thirty-five times. The shift is abrupt and deliberate; whatever one concludes from it, an English reader should at least be able to see it happen.
  • v7 "shaped the human of dust from the ground" — Heb. va-yitser et-ha'adam 'aphar min-ha'adamah. Two things English drops. First, yatsar is the potter's verb — the word used of a craftsman throwing clay, not of a decree. Second, adam (human) and adamah (ground) are the same word twice: he is an earthling from the earth, a groundling from the ground. Every English translation loses this, and it is the key to the whole chapter — the man is made of the stuff he is told to serve, and in 3:19 he goes back into it.
  • v7 "the breath of lives" — nishmat chayyim, plural. Not a slip; Hebrew often speaks of life in the plural, the way we say "riches."
  • v7 "became a living soul" — nephesh chayyah, the identical phrase used of the sea creatures, birds, and cattle in 1:20–30. The King James prints "living creature" there and "living soul" here. Same two words. The human's distinction in this verse is not the soul — the animals have that too — it is the breath, blown in personally.
  • v8 "a garden in Eden" — gan be-'eden. Eden is not a place-name meaning "garden"; as a common noun it carries luxuriance, delight, abundance. And "paradise" is not in this text at all: that word entered through Greek paradeisos, borrowed from Persian, meaning a walled royal park.
  • v9 "the knowing of good and evil" — tov wa-ra, a merism like "heaven and earth" in 1:1: naming two poles to mean the whole range between them. Closer to knowing everything there is to know than to a lesson in ethics.
  • v15 "to serve it and to keep it" — le-'ovdah u-le-shomrah. 'Avad is to serve, to labour for, and in religious contexts to worship; shamar is to guard, to keep watch over. "Till it and keep it" is not wrong but has gone soft. The man is placed in the garden as its servant and its watchman — and note that he was made to serve the ground back in v5, before there was a garden at all.

One wrinkle worth stating rather than hiding: both suffixes on those verbs are feminine (-ah, "it"), but gan, garden, is a masculine noun. Strictly, they do not agree with it. Some readers take them as pointing back to adamah, the ground, which is feminine — serve her and keep her. The Hebrew is untidy here and the English cannot show it. - v17 "dying you shall die" — mot tamut, an infinitive absolute doubling the verb for force. It is the formula of a legal death sentence, the phrasing a court uses: he shall surely be put to death. Not "you will become mortal." A verdict. - v18 "a help as his counterpart" — 'ezer ke-negdo, two words that have been mistranslated into an entire social order. 'Ezer is help or rescue, and it is used of God more often than of anyone else — the LORD is my helper — so it carries no subordination whatsoever. Ke-negdo is "like, opposite him," "corresponding to him," one standing face to face with him. "Helpmeet" and "helpmate" are not translations; they are an English accident, from the King James phrase an help meet for him, where "meet" meant suitable. - v21 "one of his sides" — tsela. The word means side — it is what the tabernacle has, what a hill has, what a building has. It means "rib" nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible. Rendered "rib" here because the Greek and then the Latin chose a narrower word, and English inherited it. "Side" also makes better sense of v23: the point is that she is the matching half of a whole that was split. - v22 "built" — banah, the verb for constructing a building, used of no other creature. The man is shaped like pottery; the woman is built like architecture. - v23 "Woman … Man" — ishshah from ish. The pun survives into English better than most, which is why it is kept, but the Hebrew is tighter: one is the other with a syllable added. - v25 "naked" — 'arummim. Hold on to the sound of this word; 3:1 opens with 'arum, and the joke is deliberate. There is a further detail only the Hebrew shows: 2:25 spells it 'arummim, matching the serpent's word almost exactly, but when they see their nakedness in 3:7 it is spelled 'erummim — the same word, written differently. The pun is set up with one spelling and paid off with another.

chapters.title: The Shrewd One, and the Going Out
chapters.html:
Genesis 3

1Now the serpent was shrewder than every living thing of the field that the LORD God had made. And it said to the woman, "So God has said, 'You shall not eat from any tree of the garden'?"

2And the woman said to the serpent, "From the fruit of the trees of the garden we may eat.

3But from the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of the garden, God has said, 'You shall not eat from it, and you shall not touch it, lest you die.'"

4And the serpent said to the woman, "Dying, you shall not die.

5For God knows that on the day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil."

6And the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and the tree was desirable for gaining insight; and she took from its fruit and ate, and she gave also to her man with her, and he ate.

7And the eyes of the two of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves coverings.

The Voice in the Garden

8And they heard the sound of the LORD God walking about in the garden at the breeze of the day, and the human and his woman hid themselves from the face of the LORD God among the trees of the garden.

9And the LORD God called to the human and said to him, "Where are you?"

10And he said, "I heard Your sound in the garden, and I was afraid, because I am naked, and I hid myself."

11And He said, "Who told you that you are naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I charged you not to eat from?"

12And the human said, "The woman whom You gave to be with me — she gave me from the tree, and I ate."

13And the LORD God said to the woman, "What is this you have done?" And the woman said, "The serpent deceived me, and I ate."

The Sentences

14And the LORD God said to the serpent, "Because you have done this, cursed are you above all cattle and above every living thing of the field. Upon your belly you shall go, and dust you shall eat all the days of your life.

15And I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. He shall strike at your head, and you shall strike at his heel."

16To the woman He said, "I will greatly increase your pain and your conceiving; in pain you shall bear children. And toward your man shall be your longing, and he shall rule over you."

17And to the human He said, "Because you listened to the voice of your woman and ate from the tree that I charged you, saying, 'You shall not eat from it' — cursed is the ground on your account. In pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life.

18And thorn and thistle it shall sprout for you, and you shall eat the plants of the field.

19By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, until you return to the ground, for from it you were taken. For dust you are, and to dust you shall return."

20And the human called his woman's name Living, because she was the mother of all living.

21And the LORD God made for the human and for his woman tunics of skin, and clothed them.

22And the LORD God said, "Look — the human has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. And now, lest he put out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever —"

23So the LORD God sent him away from the garden of Eden, to serve the ground from which he had been taken.

24And He drove the human out, and He made dwell east of the garden of Eden the cherubim, and the flame of the turning sword, to keep the way to the tree of life.

Notes

  • v1 "shrewder" — Heb. 'arum. The chapter before ended with the man and woman 'arummim, naked. The two words sound nearly identical and are unrelated in meaning. Hebrew narrative works by this kind of hinge, and it is doing real work: the story turns on nakedness and on cunning, and the writer has bolted them together with a pun on the seam between two chapters. No English translation can carry it; the note is the only place it survives.
  • v1 "shrewd" — 'arum is not a wicked word. Proverbs uses it approvingly, of the prudent man who sees trouble coming. "Crafty" and "subtle" import a verdict the Hebrew has not yet passed.
  • v1 "the serpent" — nachash. An ordinary snake; it is called one of the animals "the LORD God had made," in this same verse. Nothing in this chapter identifies it with anything else. Later traditions do; the text does not, and the note's job is to say where the text stops.
  • v1 "So God has said…?" — the Hebrew opening aph ki is broken and hard to construe, almost a half-sentence — something like "so, then, God said…?" It is not the smooth question English Bibles supply. The serpent begins mid-insinuation, and it begins by overstating the rule so the woman will correct it.
  • v3 "and you shall not touch it" — this was not in the command. Compare 2:17. Someone has added a fence around the law, and the text lets it stand without comment.
  • v4 "Dying, you shall not die" — lo mot temutun, the serpent taking God's exact construction from 2:17 (mot tamut) and putting a negative in front of it. It is not making a new claim; it is quoting the sentence back with one word changed.
  • v5 "like gods" — k-elohim, with a plural participle following. Elohim is grammatically plural and means both "God" and "gods," and the grammar here leans plural. In v22 God says the human "has become like one of us," which points the same direction. Most English Bibles print "like God"; the Hebrew is genuinely ambiguous and the ambiguity is worth preserving rather than resolving.
  • v6 "desirable for gaining insight" — nechmad le-haskil. Haskil is to gain skill, to succeed through understanding. The appeal is not appetite but competence — the wish to be good at existing.
  • v8 "the sound of the LORD God walking about" — qol YHWH Elohim mithhallekh. Qol is sound or voice; mithhallekh is the form used of strolling, moving about habitually. And "the breeze of the day" is le-ruach hayom — the same ruach that hovered over the water in 1:2, here just the evening wind. The scene is domestic: someone taking a familiar walk at the cool part of the day.
  • v9 "Where are you?" — ayyekkah. One word in Hebrew.
  • v15 "He shall strike at your head, and you shall strike at his heel" — the same verb, shuph, is used both times, and nobody is certain what it means. Proposals run from "crush" to "snap at" to "lie in wait for." English Bibles often print two different verbs — bruise the head, strike the heel — which manufactures a distinction the Hebrew does not make. One word, twice, meaning uncertain: that is the honest report.
  • v16 "your pain and your conceiving" — 'itsavon is the word here, and it is the same word used of the man in v17 for his labour in the field. English usually prints "pain" for her and "toil" for him, which splits one Hebrew word into two English ones and hides that the two sentences are built from the same material.
  • v16 "your longing" — teshuqah, a rare word, occurring three times in the Bible. One of the other three is 4:7, where sin's teshuqah is toward Cain and he must rule over it. Readers should know the nearest parallel and be left to weigh it.
  • v17 "cursed is the ground on your account" — the ground, adamah, is cursed; the man, adam, is not. Neither is the woman. In this chapter only the serpent and the soil are cursed directly.
  • v19 "for dust you are, and to dust you shall return" — closing the loop from 2:7, where he was shaped of dust from the ground. The sentence is not an added punishment so much as the undoing of an assembly.
  • v20 "Living" — Heb. Chavvah, from chay, alive. English "Eve" comes through Greek and Latin and has become a name with no meaning attached. In Hebrew it is a common word, and v20 explains itself: he calls her Living because she is the mother of all living. Rendered as the word it is, so the explanation makes sense.
  • v22 — the sentence breaks off unfinished: "lest he put out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever —". Hebrew leaves it hanging. Most English Bibles close it with a dash or supply an ending. The break is in the original.
  • v24 "to keep the way" — lishmor, the same verb given to the man in 2:15, where he was put in the garden to serve it and to keep it. He was the garden's guard. Now the garden is guarded from him, and the job he was given is being done by something else. One word closes the circle, and English uses "keep" in both places without anything marking that it is the same assignment changing hands.
  • v24 "the cherubim" — ha-keruvim, and note the definite article: "the cherubim," at this word's first appearance in the Bible, as though the reader already knows what they are.

Almost everywhere else in the Hebrew Bible the word names a made object. Cherubim are hammered out of gold on the cover of the ark, carved from olive wood and overlaid for the temple, woven into curtains, engraved on walls and doors. Exodus, Kings, and Chronicles together account for over eighty such occurrences — every one of them a manufactured thing. In the surrounding cultures, winged composite guardian figures were statues set flanking a doorway to guard it, which is exactly what this verse describes. Ezekiel's visions, by contrast, show cherubim that move and fly. Genesis does not say which these are.

What the grammar does settle is how many things are stationed. The object marker et appears twice — et ha-keruvim and et lahat ha-cherev — so the cherubim and the flame of the turning sword are the two direct objects of "He stationed," and they are what does the guarding. No third party stands in the sentence, and no hand holds the sword.

Read them as made figures and the verse does not empty out; it locks into place. Exodus 25 has Israel hammer two cherubim of gold from the ends of the ark's cover, wings spread over it, faces toward each other — and then God says, I will meet with you there, and I will speak with you from above the cover, from between the two cherubim. Cherubim of beaten gold are not an absence. They mark the exact spot where God says He will be found. Exodus 26 then has cherubim worked into the veil, the curtain across the one doorway in Israel's worship that must not be walked through.

Which is this verse. A threshold that may not be crossed, marked by cherubim, with the way to life on the other side. Eden's gate and the Holy of Holies are the same arrangement, and everything Israel later builds to approach God is built in the shape of the door they were put out of.

English "cherubim" carries none of this, and misleads further still: the word now summons the winged infants of Renaissance painting, an image with no basis in any of these texts. - v24 "the flame of the turning sword" — lahat ha-cherev ha-mithhappeket, a sword-flame that turns itself every way. Grammatically it stands on its own, not held by anyone.

chapters.title: Cain and Vapor
chapters.html:
Genesis 4

1And the human knew Eve his woman, and she conceived and bore Cain, and she said, "I have gotten a man with the LORD."

2And she bore again, his brother Vapor. And Vapor was a herder of flocks, and Cain was a worker of the ground.

3And it came to pass at the end of days that Cain brought from the fruit of the ground an offering to the LORD.

4And Vapor, he too brought from the firstborn of his flock, from their fat portions. And the LORD looked upon Vapor and upon his offering,

5but upon Cain and upon his offering He did not look. And it burned in Cain greatly, and his face fell.

6And the LORD said to Cain, "Why has it burned in you, and why has your face fallen?

7Is it not so — if you do well, lifting up; and if you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door. And toward you is its longing, but you — you must rule over it."

The Field

8And Cain said to Vapor his brother… And it came to pass, when they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Vapor his brother and killed him.

9And the LORD said to Cain, "Where is Vapor your brother?" And he said, "I do not know. Am I my brother's keeper?"

10And He said, "What have you done? The voice of your brother's bloods is crying out to Me from the ground.

11And now, cursed are you from the ground, which opened its mouth to take your brother's bloods from your hand.

12When you work the ground, it will not go on giving its strength to you. A wanderer and a wavering one you shall be in the earth."

13And Cain said to the LORD, "My guilt is greater than I can carry.

14Look — You have driven me out this day from upon the face of the ground, and from Your face I shall be hidden; and I shall be a wanderer and a wavering one in the earth, and it will be that whoever finds me will kill me."

15And the LORD said to him, "Therefore, whoever kills Cain, sevenfold it shall be avenged." And the LORD set a sign for Cain, so that whoever found him would not strike him.

16And Cain went out from before the face of the LORD, and dwelt in the land of Wandering, east of Eden.

The Line of Cain

17And Cain knew his woman, and she conceived and bore Enoch. And he was building a city, and he called the name of the city after the name of his son, Enoch.

18And to Enoch was born Irad, and Irad fathered Mehujael, and Mehujael fathered Methushael, and Methushael fathered Lamech.

19And Lamech took for himself two women: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the second, Zillah.

20And Adah bore Jabal; he was the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock.

21And the name of his brother was Jubal; he was the father of all who handle the lyre and the pipe.

22And Zillah, she too bore Tubal-cain, a sharpener of every cutting tool of bronze and iron. And the sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah.

23And Lamech said to his women,
"Adah and Zillah, hear my voice;
women of Lamech, give ear to my saying.
For a man I have killed for wounding me,
and a boy for bruising me.

24For sevenfold Cain is avenged,
and Lamech seventy-seven."

25And the human knew his woman again, and she bore a son and called his name Seth, "for God has set for me another seed in place of Vapor, because Cain killed him."

26And to Seth also a son was born, and he called his name Enosh. Then it was begun, calling on the name of the LORD.

Notes

  • v1 "Cain" — Heb. Qayin, and Eve's word for what she has done is qaniti, "I have gotten / acquired / produced." The name and the verb chime. She is not describing him; she is punning on him.
  • v1 "a man with the LORD" — ish et-YHWH, three words that nobody can settle. Et is either the preposition "with" or the untranslatable particle Hebrew puts before a direct object. So the line reads "I have gotten a man with the LORD's help," or "I have gotten a man, namely the LORD," or "I have gotten a man along with the LORD." English Bibles pick one and print it smoothly. The Hebrew does not resolve, and the first thing a mother says about the first child born is genuinely unclear.
  • v2 "Vapor" — Heb. Hevel. This is the name English prints as "Abel," which means nothing to an English reader. In Hebrew it is a common noun: vapor, breath, mist, the thing that is gone as you name it. It is the word that opens Ecclesiastes — hevel havelim, usually "vanity of vanities," better "breath of breaths." The second human being born is named Fleeting, and he lasts eight verses. Rendered as the word it is, because "Abel" hides the entire joke and the entire grief.
  • v2 "a worker of the ground" — 'oved adamah, the same pairing from 2:5 and 2:15, where the human was made to serve the ground. Cain is doing what humans were made for. That is worth holding on to when the offering is refused: the text gives no reason, and the older reader's instinct to supply one — wrong attitude, wrong produce — is the reader's, not the text's.
  • v5 "it burned in Cain" — va-yichar le-Qayin, literally "and it burned to Cain." Hebrew locates anger as heat inside a person, with no stated subject. "Cain was very angry" is accurate and colder than the Hebrew.
  • v7 — one of the hardest verses in the book, and no honest rendering is smooth. "If you do well, lifting up" is three words in Hebrew, se'et, an infinitive with no object; lifting of the face, probably, answering the fallen face in v5, but it is not said.
  • v7 "sin is crouching at the door" — robets, a participle used of an animal lying in wait. There is an Akkadian word, rabisu, naming a demon that lurks at doorways, and the resemblance is close enough that many readers hear a crouching thing rather than an abstraction. Note also that sin is feminine in Hebrew while crouching here is masculine — the grammar is already uneven, which is part of why the verse is so contested.
  • v7 "toward you is its longing, but you must rule over it" — teshuqah and mashal, the same two words as 3:16, where the woman's longing is toward her man and he rules over her. Four verses apart in a short book, the identical uncommon pair. Whatever it means in one place constrains what it can mean in the other, and English translations that print "desire" in 3:16 and something else here sever the link.
  • v8 "And Cain said to Vapor his brother…" — the Hebrew has the verb va-yomer, "and he said," and then no speech. The sentence moves straight to the field. Three things are worth knowing, and none of them is that the text is damaged.

First, it may be deliberate. The words Cain used to get his brother alone are withheld from the reader. That would not be out of character for this writer: 3:22 breaks off God's own sentence unfinished — "lest he put out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever —" — at the moment of greatest weight. Twice in two chapters, language is cut away exactly where the reader most wants it. Once is an accident; twice looks like a hand. The ellipsis here is an attempt to let the English reader feel the withholding instead of having it explained.

Second, most published Bibles simply render it "Cain spoke with his brother" or "talked with Abel his brother," reading amar el as conversed with rather than as introducing a quotation. On that reading nothing is missing at all: the verse reports that a conversation happened and does not undertake to quote it. This is the King James reading and it is grammatically defensible.

Third, several ancient translations — Samaritan, Greek, Latin, Syriac — supply "let us go out to the field," and some modern Bibles print that with a footnote. Whether the Hebrew lost the line or the translations added it is contested, and the usual principle that the harder reading is the older one argues the Hebrew here is original. - v10 "your brother's bloods" — demei, plural. Hebrew uses the plural of blood for bloodshed, blood that has been spilled and is owed. Not a poetic flourish; a legal one. - v12 "a wanderer and a wavering one" — na' va-nad, a rhyming pair like tohu wa-vohu in 1:2. The sound is half the meaning. And in v16 he goes to the land of Nod — the same root again. He is sentenced to a word, and then he moves to it. - v13 "My guilt is greater than I can carry" — 'avoni, which means both the iniquity and the punishment for it, and nasa, which means both to bear and to forgive. So the line is simultaneously "my punishment is too heavy" and "my guilt is too great to be forgiven." English must choose. Hebrew does not, and Cain's first words after the murder are a sentence that can be read as self-pity or as confession. - v15 "a sign for Cain" — 'ot le-Qayin, a sign for him, not necessarily on him. The Hebrew never says it was put on his body; "the mark of Cain" is a later reading hardened into an English idiom. A sign given to someone, for their protection, is the plain sense, and the verse says the sign's purpose is to stop people killing him — it is a mercy, not a brand. - v23–24 Lamech's song — the first poetry spoken by a human being in the Bible, and it is a boast about killing a boy. Set as lines because the Hebrew is parallel verse. Where God set Cain's avenging at sevenfold, Lamech claims seventy-seven for himself: five generations from the first murder, the arithmetic of revenge has multiplied elevenfold, and nobody has commented on it. - v26 "Then it was begun" — az huchal, a passive with no subject. Something started; the text does not say who started it.

chapters.title: The Begettings of Adam, and the Drumbeat
chapters.html:
Genesis 5

1This is the book of the begettings of Adam. In the day God created humankind, in the likeness of God He made him.

2Male and female He created them, and He blessed them and called their name Humankind in the day they were created.

3And Adam lived a hundred and thirty years, and he fathered in his likeness, according to his image, and called his name Seth.

4And the days of Adam after he fathered Seth were eight hundred years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

5And all the days of Adam that he lived were nine hundred and thirty years. And he died.

6And Seth lived a hundred and five years, and he fathered Enosh.

7And Seth lived after he fathered Enosh eight hundred and seven years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

8And all the days of Seth were nine hundred and twelve years. And he died.

9And Enosh lived ninety years, and he fathered Kenan.

10And Enosh lived after he fathered Kenan eight hundred and fifteen years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

11And all the days of Enosh were nine hundred and five years. And he died.

12And Kenan lived seventy years, and he fathered Mahalalel.

13And Kenan lived after he fathered Mahalalel eight hundred and forty years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

14And all the days of Kenan were nine hundred and ten years. And he died.

15And Mahalalel lived sixty-five years, and he fathered Jared.

16And Mahalalel lived after he fathered Jared eight hundred and thirty years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

17And all the days of Mahalalel were eight hundred and ninety-five years. And he died.

18And Jared lived a hundred and sixty-two years, and he fathered Enoch.

19And Jared lived after he fathered Enoch eight hundred years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

20And all the days of Jared were nine hundred and sixty-two years. And he died.

The One Who Was Not

21And Enoch lived sixty-five years, and he fathered Methuselah.

22And Enoch walked with God after he fathered Methuselah three hundred years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

23And all the days of Enoch were three hundred and sixty-five years.

24And Enoch walked with God. And he was not, for God took him.

25And Methuselah lived a hundred and eighty-seven years, and he fathered Lamech.

26And Methuselah lived after he fathered Lamech seven hundred and eighty-two years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

27And all the days of Methuselah were nine hundred and sixty-nine years. And he died.

28And Lamech lived a hundred and eighty-two years, and he fathered a son.

29And he called his name Noah, saying, "This one will bring us relief from our work and from the pain of our hands, out of the ground which the LORD has cursed."

30And Lamech lived after he fathered Noah five hundred and ninety-five years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

31And all the days of Lamech were seven hundred and seventy-seven years. And he died.

32And Noah was five hundred years old, and Noah fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

Notes

  • v1 "the book of the begettings" — sepher toledot, the same structuring word as 2:4, now with sepher, a written document, in front of it. This is the only place in Genesis that calls a section a book, and it reads like a citation — as though a list already existed and is being copied in.
  • v2 "called their name Humankind" — adam, the same word that has been the man's name since chapter 2, given here to both of them together, male and female, as a single name. English prints "Adam" in v3 and "man" or "mankind" in v2, which conceals that it is one word doing both jobs. The species and the individual are named identically, and v2 says the name belongs to the pair.
  • v3 "in his likeness, according to his image" — demut and tselem, the two words from 1:26, now used of Adam fathering Seth. What God did in making humankind is what a human does in having a child. The echo is exact and deliberate, and it is the chapter's quietest claim.
  • The repetition — the formula runs: lived X years, fathered N, lived Y more years, fathered sons and daughters, all his days were Z, and he died. Eight times. It is monotonous on purpose; the spec for this project says a genealogy is supposed to be monotonous, and smoothing it out would destroy the effect. Read aloud, the phrase and he died lands like a drum. Nothing else in the chapter is trying to happen.
  • vv21–24 Enoch — and then the drum stops. Enoch's entry is the shortest life in the chapter, and its closing formula is missing. Instead of and he died, it says and he was not, for God took him. The chapter has spent twenty verses training the reader to expect three words, and then withholds them. That is the whole point of the repetition: it exists to be broken once.
  • v22, 24 "walked with God" — hithhallekh et-ha-Elohim, the reflexive form of the verb, the same form used in 3:8 of God walking about in the garden at the breeze of the day. Whatever Adam lost the ability to be near, Enoch is described as doing alongside it.
  • v24 "and he was not" — ve-einennu, a flat negation of existence. Not "he departed," not "he was taken up" — and he was not. The taking is stated in the next clause, but the first thing said is simply his absence.
  • v29 "Noah … relief" — Lamech explains the name from yenachamenu, "he will comfort/relieve us," from the root nacham. But the name Noach comes from a different root, nuach, to rest. It is a loose pun, not an etymology, and Hebrew naming does this constantly — the sound is close enough, and the meaning is what the parent wants to say. Noting it because a reader who checks will find the mismatch and wonder whether the translation erred. It did not; the text is punning.
  • v29 "the pain of our hands" — 'itsavon, the same word as the sentences in 3:16 and 3:17. Lamech is quoting the curse. And he names his son for the end of it, three chapters before the flood.
  • The ages — the Hebrew, Greek, and Samaritan traditions of Genesis do not agree on the numbers in this chapter; the totals and the begetting-ages differ substantially between them. The figures here follow the Hebrew. That the traditions diverge is a plain fact worth knowing; which is original is not something this rendering can settle, and no attempt is made to reconcile them.

chapters.title: The Ruin of the Earth, and the Box
chapters.html:
Genesis 6

1And it came to pass, when humankind began to be many upon the face of the ground, and daughters were born to them,

2that the sons of God saw the daughters of humankind, that they were good, and they took for themselves women from all whom they chose.

3And the LORD said, "My breath shall not abide in the human forever, in that he also is flesh. And his days shall be a hundred and twenty years."

4The fallen ones were in the earth in those days, and also afterward, when the sons of God came in to the daughters of humankind and they bore to them. These are the mighty ones who were of old, the men of the name.

The Grief

5And the LORD saw that the evil of humankind was great in the earth, and that every shaping of the thoughts of his heart was only evil all the day.

6And the LORD was sorry that He had made humankind in the earth, and it grieved Him to His heart.

7And the LORD said, "I will wipe away the human whom I created from upon the face of the ground — from human to cattle, to creeping thing, and to the bird of the heavens — for I am sorry that I made them."

8But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.

The Begettings of Noah

9These are the begettings of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, whole in his generations. With God Noah walked.

10And Noah fathered three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

11And the earth was ruined before God, and the earth was filled with violence.

12And God saw the earth, and look — it was ruined, for all flesh had ruined its way upon the earth.

13And God said to Noah, "The end of all flesh has come before Me, for the earth is filled with violence because of them. And look — I am ruining them, along with the earth.

14Make yourself a box of gopher wood. Rooms you shall make in the box, and you shall cover it inside and out with the covering.

15And this is how you shall make it: three hundred cubits the length of the box, fifty cubits its width, and thirty cubits its height.

16A light you shall make for the box, and to a cubit you shall finish it from above. And the opening of the box you shall set in its side. Lower, second, and third decks you shall make it.

17And I — look, I am bringing the flood, waters upon the earth, to ruin all flesh in which is the breath of life from under the heavens. Everything that is in the earth shall expire.

18But I will raise up My covenant with you, and you shall come into the box — you, and your sons, and your wife, and your sons' wives with you.

19And from every living thing, from all flesh, two of each you shall bring into the box to keep alive with you; male and female they shall be.

20From the bird after its kind, and from the cattle after its kind, from every creeping thing of the ground after its kind — two of each shall come to you, to be kept alive.

21And you, take for yourself from every food that is eaten, and gather it to yourself, and it shall be food for you and for them."

22And Noah did according to all that God commanded him. So he did.

Notes

  • v2, 4 "the sons of God" — benei ha-Elohim, exactly that, twice. The text does not say who they are. It does not explain them, condemn them by name, or return to them. Four verses, and then the subject changes and never comes back. Every account of who they were is supplied from somewhere other than these four verses.
  • v3 "My breath shall not abide" — lo yadon ruchi. Nobody knows what yadon is. The root could be din, to judge or contend, or dun, to remain or abide; neither is certain and both are argued. And the next word, beshaggam, rendered here "in that he also," is one of the genuinely opaque words in Genesis. This verse is unclear in Hebrew and the English should not pretend otherwise.
  • v4 "the fallen ones" — ha-nephilim. Most English Bibles transliterate it, which turns an ordinary-looking Hebrew word into a proper noun and a mystery. The form looks like it belongs to the root naphal, to fall, so "fallen ones" — but that is what the word looks like, not a translation anyone can prove. Rendered as what it appears to say, with the uncertainty stated here rather than hidden behind a capital letter.
  • v4 "the men of the name" — anshei ha-shem. Usually "men of renown," which is what it means. Worth hearing literally anyway, because five chapters later a group of men will try to build a tower and make themselves a name.
  • v6 "was sorry… it grieved Him" — two words that both reach backward. Va-yinnachem, from nacham, is the root Lamech used when he named Noah in 5:29, saying this one will bring us relief. The father named his son for comfort; now God is "comforted" in the sense of relenting, and the flood follows. And va-yit'atsev, "it grieved Him," is from 'atsav — the same root as 'itsavon, the pain given to the woman and the man in 3:16–17. The word for the curse laid on humankind is now the word for what humankind does to God. That is not a coincidence available to an English reader, and it is the center of the chapter.
  • v8 "Noah found favor" — Noach matsa chen. In Hebrew, Noach is written nun-chet and chen, favor, is written chet-nun. The same two letters, reversed. The sentence that saves him is his own name turned around.
  • v9 "whole in his generations" — tamim, the word used of an animal fit for sacrifice: unblemished, entire, without defect. Not "morally perfect" — sound, complete, all there.
  • v9 "With God Noah walked" — et ha-Elohim hithhallekh Noach, the same construction used of Enoch in 5:22 and 5:24, the man who did not die. Two men in the book are described this way, and this is the second.
  • vv11–13 "ruined… ruined… ruining" — the root shachat four times in three verses: the earth was ruined, God saw it was ruined, all flesh had ruined its way, and God says I am ruining them. English prints "corrupt" for the crime and "destroy" for the punishment, which conceals that they are the same word. The judgment is not a response to the ruin; it is the ruin, handed back.
  • v11 "violence" — chamas. Not warfare specifically — lawlessness, the violent seizure of what is not yours. It is the word the prophets use for what the strong do to the poor.
  • v14 "a box" — tevah. This is not the word for a ship, a boat, or any vessel that sails; Hebrew has those words and does not use them here. A tevah is a chest, a box, a container. The only other object in the whole Hebrew Bible called a tevah is the basket of reeds that Moses' mother waterproofs and sets in the river. Two objects, two rescues through water, one rare word. "Ark" comes from Latin arca, a chest — so the English is right, but four centuries of use have made it sound like a ship, and it is a box that floats.
  • v14 "gopher wood" — atsei gopher. The word gopher occurs here and nowhere else in Hebrew. No one knows what tree it was. Transliterating it is the honest option.
  • v14 "cover it… with the covering" — ve-khapharta… ba-kopher, the verb and the noun from the same root. Kopher is pitch, the black tar you seal a hull with. It is also the root of kippur — atonement, as in the Day of Atonement. The verb means to cover over, and what it covers is either a boat's seams or a people's guilt. Here, at its first appearance in the Bible, it is literal tar on literal wood.
  • v16 "a light" — tsohar, another word whose meaning is not settled: possibly a window, possibly a roof, possibly something that gives light. And "to a cubit you shall finish it from above" is obscure in the Hebrew as it stands. The building instructions are less clear than English translations make them.
  • v17 "the flood" — mabbul, a rare word used almost exclusively of this event. Not the ordinary word for a flood or an overflowing river. Whatever this is, Hebrew gives it its own name.

chapters.title: The Undoing of the Second Day
chapters.html:
Genesis 7

1And the LORD said to Noah, "Come, you and all your household, into the box, for you I have seen righteous before Me in this generation.

2From all the clean cattle you shall take for yourself seven and seven, a man and his woman; and from the cattle that are not clean, two, a man and his woman.

3Also from the bird of the heavens, seven and seven, male and female, to keep seed alive upon the face of all the earth.

4For in seven more days I will send rain upon the earth forty days and forty nights, and I will wipe away every standing thing that I have made from upon the face of the ground."

5And Noah did according to all that the LORD commanded him.

6And Noah was six hundred years old, and the flood came — waters upon the earth.

7And Noah came, and his sons, and his wife, and his sons' wives with him, into the box, from before the waters of the flood.

8From the clean cattle, and from the cattle that are not clean, and from the bird, and everything that creeps upon the ground,

9two by two they came to Noah, into the box, male and female, as God had commanded Noah.

The Day the Deep Broke Open

10And it came to pass after the seven days that the waters of the flood were upon the earth.

11In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month — on that day all the fountains of the great deep were split open, and the lattices of the heavens were opened.

12And the rain was upon the earth forty days and forty nights.

13On the bone of that same day Noah came, and Shem and Ham and Japheth the sons of Noah, and Noah's wife and the three wives of his sons with them, into the box —

14they, and every living thing after its kind, and every beast after its kind, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth after its kind, and every bird after its kind, every winged thing of every wing.

15And they came to Noah, into the box, two by two from all flesh in which is the breath of life.

16And those that came, male and female from all flesh they came, as God had commanded him. And the LORD shut him in.

17And the flood was forty days upon the earth, and the waters multiplied and lifted the box, and it rose high above the earth.

18And the waters overpowered and multiplied greatly upon the earth, and the box went upon the face of the waters.

19And the waters overpowered exceedingly, exceedingly upon the earth, and all the high mountains under all the heavens were covered.

20Fifteen cubits above them the waters overpowered, and the mountains were covered.

21And all flesh expired that creeps upon the earth — in the bird, and in the cattle, and in the living thing, and in every swarming thing that swarms upon the earth, and every human.

22Everything in whose nostrils was the breath of the spirit of life, of all that was on the dry ground, died.

23And He wiped away every standing thing that was upon the face of the ground, from human to cattle, to creeping thing, and to the bird of the heavens — and they were wiped away from the earth. And only Noah was left, and those with him in the box.

24And the waters overpowered upon the earth a hundred and fifty days.

Notes

  • v2 "seven and seven… two" — the text says seven pairs of clean animals and two of unclean. In 6:19 the instruction was two of every kind without distinction. Both stand in the Hebrew, four verses apart, and neither is a translation artifact. Reported rather than harmonized.
  • v2 "a man and his woman" — ish ve-ishto, the ordinary Hebrew for a husband and wife, used here of livestock. Not "male and female," which is the phrase v3 switches to for the birds. The animals come aboard as couples in the same words the book used for the first two humans.
  • v4 "every standing thing" — ha-yequm, from the root qum, to stand up or arise. A rare word meaning roughly "all that stands," everything that has risen into existence. English usually prints "living substance" or "living thing," which is close but loses the picture of things standing that are about to be flattened.
  • v11 "all the fountains of the great deep were split open, and the lattices of the heavens were opened" — the single most important sentence in the chapter, and English translations generally soften it. Tehom, the deep, is the same word as 1:2, the dark water God divided on the second day of creation by hammering out an expanse between the waters below and the waters above. Here that expanse fails from both directions at once: the deep below is split open — nivqe'u, a violent verb, used of cracking wood and splitting a rock — and the heavens above are opened. This is not weather. It is day two running backwards, and the created order coming apart along the seam where it was made.
  • v11 "lattices" — arubbot, the word for a latticed opening, a smoke-hole, a dovecote. "Floodgates" is an interpretation; "windows" is closer. The sky is a screen with holes in it, and they have been unstopped.
  • v13 "on the bone of that same day" — be-'etsem ha-yom ha-zeh, literally "in the bone of this day." Hebrew idiom for on that very day, and it is kept literal here because the image is exactly right: the day's own bone, its hard center.
  • vv17–20 "overpowered" — gavar, four times, a verb of military dominance: to prevail, to be mighty, to overcome. English prints "increased" and "prevailed," but the word is the same each time and it is a word about strength, not volume. The waters are not rising; they are winning.
  • v19 "exceedingly, exceedingly" — me'od me'od, the word doubled. The last time me'od appeared in this book was 1:31, where God looked at everything He had made and it was tov me'od, very good. The intensifier returns, twice over, for the water.
  • v16 "And the LORD shut him in" — va-yisgor YHWH ba'ado, four words, and they are the last thing said before the rain. Noah does not close the door. The verse also quietly changes the divine name: God, Elohim, gave the command in the first half of the same sentence; it is the LORD, YHWH, who shuts the door.
  • v22 "the breath of the spirit of life" — nishmat ruach chayyim, stacking the word for breath from 2:7 with the word for spirit/wind from 1:2. The two words that made the human alive are named together at the moment everything with them dies.
  • v23 "wiped away… wiped away" — va-yimach… va-yimmachu, active then passive, the verb God promised in 6:7 and 7:4 now carried out. Machah is the word for wiping a dish or blotting writing off a scroll. The earth is being erased, not drowned.

chapters.title: God Remembered, and the Box Rested
chapters.html:
Genesis 8

1And God remembered Noah, and every living thing and every beast that was with him in the box. And God made a wind pass over the earth, and the waters grew quiet.

2And the fountains of the deep were stopped up, and the lattices of the heavens, and the rain from the heavens was shut in.

3And the waters returned from upon the earth, going and returning; and the waters diminished at the end of a hundred and fifty days.

4And the box rested, in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, upon the mountains of Ararat.

5And the waters went on going and diminishing until the tenth month; in the tenth, on the first of the month, the heads of the mountains were seen.

The Raven and the Dove

6And it came to pass at the end of forty days that Noah opened the window of the box that he had made,

7and he sent out the raven; and it went out, going out and returning, until the waters dried up from upon the earth.

8And he sent out the dove from him, to see whether the waters had lightened from upon the face of the ground.

9But the dove found no resting place for the sole of her foot, and she returned to him, to the box, for waters were upon the face of all the earth. And he put out his hand and took her and brought her to himself, into the box.

10And he waited yet another seven days, and again he sent out the dove from the box.

11And the dove came to him at evening time, and look — an olive leaf, freshly plucked, in her mouth. And Noah knew that the waters had lightened from upon the earth.

12And he waited yet another seven days, and he sent out the dove, and she did not return to him again.

13And it came to pass in the six hundred and first year, in the first month, on the first of the month, that the waters dried from upon the earth. And Noah removed the covering of the box and looked, and behold — the face of the ground was dry.

14And in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth was dried out.

Come Out

15And God spoke to Noah, saying,

16"Go out from the box — you, and your wife, and your sons, and your sons' wives with you.

17Every living thing that is with you, from all flesh, in the bird and in the cattle and in every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth — bring out with you, and let them swarm in the earth and be fruitful and multiply upon the earth."

18And Noah went out, and his sons, and his wife, and his sons' wives with him.

19Every living thing, every creeping thing, and every bird — everything that creeps upon the earth, by their families — went out from the box.

20And Noah built an altar to the LORD, and he took from every clean beast and from every clean bird, and he sent up burnt offerings on the altar.

21And the LORD smelled the quieting smell, and the LORD said to His heart, "I will not go on cursing the ground again on account of the human, for the shaping of the human heart is evil from his youth. And I will not go on striking every living thing again, as I have done.

22From now on, all the days of the earth —
seed and harvest,
and cold and heat,
and summer and winter,
and day and night —
shall not cease."

Notes

  • v1 "God remembered" — va-yizkor. Hebrew zakhar is not the recovery of something forgotten; it is turning toward and acting on an obligation. When God "remembers," something happens next. The word is the hinge of the flood story, and everything after this verse runs backwards toward dry land.
  • v1 "God made a wind pass over the earth" — va-ya'aver Elohim ruach al ha-aretz. Go back to 1:2: the breath of God was hovering over the face of the waters. The same word, ruach, over the same waters, at the moment the world begins again. Chapter 7 unmade the second day of creation; this verse restarts at the second verse of the book. The story is not a rescue narrative with a creation echo bolted on — it is creation, run in reverse and then forward.
  • v4 "the box rested" — va-tanach ha-tevah, from the root nuach, to rest. Which is Noah's name. The vessel Noahs onto the mountain. This is the first of four times in this chapter that his name's root surfaces in ordinary words, and no English reader can hear any of them.
  • v4 "the mountains of Ararat" — plural, harei Ararat. A range or a region, not a named peak. "Mount Ararat" is a later identification; the Hebrew does not name a mountain.
  • v7 "going out and returning" — yatso va-shov, the same doubled construction used of the waters in v3, halokh va-shov, going and returning. The raven flies the way the water moves.
  • v9 "no resting place for the sole of her foot" — manoach, and there is the root again — the same nuach as v4 and as Noah. The bird cannot find a manoach; the box has already found its rest. The dove is looking for what the man is named for.
  • v11 "freshly plucked" — taraph. The verb normally means to tear, and is used of a predator tearing prey. Here it describes a leaf torn from a tree — which tells Noah what he needs to know, because a leaf that had to be torn off was growing.
  • vv13–14 "dried… was dried out" — two different verbs. Charvu in v13 is the water drying off the surface; yavshah in v14 is the ground itself becoming dry. English tends to print "dried" twice. The Hebrew marks two stages, fifty-seven days apart.
  • v20 "sent up burnt offerings" — va-ya'al 'olot. The noun 'olah is from the verb 'alah, to go up: a burnt offering is literally a going-up, named for the smoke. The English "burnt offering" names the fire; the Hebrew names the ascent.
  • v21 "the quieting smell" — reach ha-nichoach. And there is the root a fourth time. Nichoach is from nuach, the same root as the box resting, the dove's resting place, and the man's name. English prints "a pleasing aroma" or "a sweet savour," which is the sense, but the word is built from rest. The smoke quiets something. In a chapter where God has just remembered, the man named Rest makes a smell of resting rise, and the sentence that follows is the promise never to do this again.
  • v21 "said to His heart" — el libbo. In 6:6, before the flood, it grieved Him to His heart — el libbo, the identical phrase. The same heart that was grieved into destroying now speaks to itself and stops.
  • v21 "for the shaping of the human heart is evil from his youth" — this is the most important sentence in the flood story, and it is easy to miss. In 6:5 the reason given for the flood was that every shaping of the thoughts of his heart was only evil all the day — yetser, shaping, the same word. Here that same fact is given as the reason for never doing it again. Nothing about humankind has changed. The identical diagnosis appears once as grounds for destruction and once as grounds for mercy, and the only thing between them is that God remembered.
  • v22 — set as lines because the Hebrew is four balanced pairs: seed and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night. The last pair is quoted straight out of the first chapter, where God separated them.

chapters.title: The Bow Hung Up
chapters.html:
Genesis 9

1And God blessed Noah and his sons, and said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth.

2And the fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon every living thing of the earth, and upon every bird of the heavens, upon everything that the ground creeps with, and upon all the fish of the sea. Into your hand they are given.

3Every creeping thing that is alive shall be food for you. Like the green plants, I have given you everything.

4But flesh with its soul — its blood — you shall not eat.

5And surely your blood, for your souls, I will require. From the hand of every living thing I will require it, and from the hand of the human — from the hand of a man's brother — I will require the soul of the human.

6One who sheds the blood of the human,
by the human shall his blood be shed,
for in the image of God He made the human.

7And you, be fruitful and multiply; swarm in the earth and multiply in it."

The Bow

8And God said to Noah and to his sons with him, saying,

9"And I — look, I am raising up My covenant with you, and with your seed after you,

10and with every living soul that is with you: in the bird, in the cattle, and in every living thing of the earth with you — from all that came out of the box, to every living thing of the earth.

11And I raise up My covenant with you: never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood, and never again shall there be a flood to ruin the earth."

12And God said, "This is the sign of the covenant that I am giving between Me and you and every living soul that is with you, for everlasting generations:

13My bow I have set in the cloud, and it shall be for a sign of covenant between Me and the earth.

14And it shall be, when I cloud a cloud over the earth, that the bow shall be seen in the cloud.

15And I will remember My covenant that is between Me and you and every living soul in all flesh, and never again shall the waters become a flood to ruin all flesh.

16And the bow shall be in the cloud, and I will see it, to remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living soul in all flesh that is upon the earth."

17And God said to Noah, "This is the sign of the covenant that I have raised up between Me and all flesh that is upon the earth."

The Vineyard

18And the sons of Noah who came out of the box were Shem and Ham and Japheth. And Ham, he is the father of Canaan.

19These three were the sons of Noah, and from these the whole earth was scattered.

20And Noah began — a man of the ground — and he planted a vineyard.

21And he drank from the wine and became drunk, and he uncovered himself inside his tent.

22And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father, and he told his two brothers outside.

23And Shem and Japheth took the garment and laid it on the shoulder of the two of them, and they walked backward and covered the nakedness of their father. And their faces were backward, and they did not see the nakedness of their father.

24And Noah woke from his wine, and he knew what his youngest son had done to him.

25And he said,
"Cursed be Canaan.
A servant of servants shall he be to his brothers."

26And he said,
"Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem,
and let Canaan be a servant to them.

27May God make wide for Japheth,
and let him dwell in the tents of Shem,
and let Canaan be a servant to them."

28And Noah lived after the flood three hundred and fifty years.

29And all the days of Noah were nine hundred and fifty years. And he died.

Notes

  • v1 "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth" — word for word from 1:28, the blessing on the first humans. But read what is not repeated: 1:28 continued and subdue it, and hold sway. Those two hard verbs, kavash and radah, are gone. What replaces them in v2 is fear and dread. The first humans were given rule; these are given terror. It is a colder arrangement, and the omission is the argument.
  • v3 "Every creeping thing that is alive shall be food for you" — in 1:29–30, both humans and animals were given plants. Eating meat is permitted here for the first time, and the sentence that grants it points straight back: like the green plants, I have given you everything.
  • v4 "flesh with its soul — its blood" — basar be-nafsho damo. The nephesh — the same word rendered "soul" throughout chapters 1 and 2, whose root sense is throat — is identified with the blood. The prohibition is not hygiene. It is that the life belongs to someone else, and you may have the animal but not that.
  • v5 "I will require" — edrosh, three times in one verse. The verb means to seek out, to inquire after, to go looking for. Blood is not merely avenged; it is sought, the way you search for something owed to you. The same picture as 4:10, where Abel's blood cried out from the ground.
  • v6 — set as lines because the Hebrew is a perfect mirror. Word by word: shofekh / dam / ha-adam / ba-adam / damo / yishaphekh — shedder, blood, the human, by the human, his blood, shall be shed. The sentence turns around at its middle and walks back out the way it came in, so the punishment is the crime reversed, in the shape of the line itself. No English word order can reproduce it; the lineation is an attempt to let the turn be felt.
  • v6 "by the human" — ba-adam, which can be "by a human," "in the human," or "for the human." The preposition is doing real work and is not decidable here. Whether this verse establishes human courts or states a principle about God's own requiring depends on which sense is chosen, and the Hebrew does not choose.
  • v6 "in the image of God" — be-tselem Elohim, quoting 1:27. The reason murder is intolerable is not the value of life in general; it is that the thing destroyed was a likeness.
  • v13 "My bow" — qashti. This is not a word for a rainbow. Qeshet is the war bow, the weapon — it is the word used when a soldier draws a bow throughout the Hebrew Bible, and Hebrew has no separate term for the arc in the sky. So the sentence is: My weapon I have set in the cloud. A bow hung in the clouds is a bow that has been put down, and one hung with its curve upward is a bow pointed away from the earth. English "rainbow" turns a laid-down weapon into a weather phenomenon.
  • v14 "when I cloud a cloud" — be-'anni 'anan, the verb and its noun from one root, the way Hebrew likes to do it. Kept literal because the smoothing to "when I bring clouds" loses the doubling.
  • vv15–16 "I will remember… to remember" — zakhar again, the verb from 8:1 where God remembered Noah. The sign in the sky is not for the humans to see and take comfort; both verses say it is so that God will see it and remember. The covenant's reminder points upward.
  • v20 "a man of the ground" — ish ha-adamah. Cain in 4:2 was an oved adamah, a worker of the ground. Noah, who was named for relief from the ground's curse in 5:29, becomes a man of the ground — and the first thing the restarted world produces is a drunk man naked in a tent.
  • v21 "he uncovered himself" — va-yitgal, reflexive: he uncovered himself. Not "was uncovered." What follows is his own doing first.
  • v22, 23 "nakedness" — 'ervah. The word covers ordinary nakedness and also functions in legal contexts as a term for sexual transgression, which is why v24's "what his youngest son had done to him" has been read as more than looking. The Hebrew says saw and then says done. Both words are there, and the gap between them is not filled in.
  • v25 "Cursed be Canaan" — Ham commits the act; Canaan, Ham's son, who has not appeared in the scene, receives the curse. The text states this without explaining it, and v18 and v22 both go out of their way to remind the reader whose father Ham is. Reported as it stands.
  • v27 "May God make wide for Japheth" — yapht Elohim le-Yephet, a pun: the verb yapht (make wide, make room) chimes with the name Yephet. Like Noah's own name in 5:29, the blessing is built out of the sound of the name rather than its derivation.

chapters.title: The Nations, by Their Tongues
chapters.html:
Genesis 10

1And these are the begettings of the sons of Noah — Shem, Ham, and Japheth — and sons were born to them after the flood.

Japheth

2The sons of Japheth: Gomer and Magog and Madai and Javan and Tubal and Meshech and Tiras.

3And the sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz and Riphath and Togarmah.

4And the sons of Javan: Elishah and Tarshish, Kittim and Dodanim.

5From these the coastlands of the nations separated out in their lands, each by his tongue, by their families, in their nations.

Ham

6And the sons of Ham: Cush and Egypt and Put and Canaan.

7And the sons of Cush: Seba and Havilah and Sabtah and Raamah and Sabteca. And the sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.

8And Cush fathered Nimrod. He began to be a mighty one in the earth.

9He was a mighty hunter before the LORD. Therefore it is said, "Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the LORD."

10And the beginning of his kingdom was Babel and Erech and Akkad and Calneh, in the land of Shinar.

11From that land went out Asshur, and he built Nineveh and Rehoboth-Ir and Calah,

12and Resen between Nineveh and Calah — that is the great city.

13And Egypt fathered the Ludim and the Anamim and the Lehabim and the Naphtuhim,

14and the Pathrusim and the Casluhim — from whom the Philistines went out — and the Caphtorim.

15And Canaan fathered Sidon his firstborn, and Heth,

16and the Jebusite and the Amorite and the Girgashite,

17and the Hivite and the Arkite and the Sinite,

18and the Arvadite and the Zemarite and the Hamathite. And afterward the families of the Canaanite were scattered.

19And the border of the Canaanite was from Sidon, as you come toward Gerar, as far as Gaza; as you come toward Sodom and Gomorrah and Admah and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha.

20These are the sons of Ham, by their families, by their tongues, in their lands, in their nations.

Shem

21And to Shem, to him also, children were born — the father of all the sons of Eber, the brother of Japheth the elder.

22The sons of Shem: Elam and Asshur and Arpachshad and Lud and Aram.

23And the sons of Aram: Uz and Hul and Gether and Mash.

24And Arpachshad fathered Shelah, and Shelah fathered Eber.

25And to Eber were born two sons. The name of the one was Division, for in his days the earth was divided; and the name of his brother was Joktan.

26And Joktan fathered Almodad and Sheleph and Hazarmaveth and Jerah,

27and Hadoram and Uzal and Diklah,

28and Obal and Abimael and Sheba,

29and Ophir and Havilah and Jobab. All these were the sons of Joktan.

30And their dwelling was from Mesha, as you come toward Sephar, the mountain of the east.

31These are the sons of Shem, by their families, by their tongues, in their lands, by their nations.

32These are the families of the sons of Noah, by their begettings, in their nations. And from these the nations separated out in the earth after the flood.

Notes

  • vv5, 20, 31 "by their tongues" — li-lshonotam, three times, once at the close of each branch. The nations here already have separate languages, and they already have separate lands. The next chapter opens with the whole earth speaking one lip and one set of words, and ends with languages being divided at Babel. The two chapters do not run in sequence. Chapter 10 is the outcome; chapter 11 goes back and tells how it happened. Hebrew narrative does this often — finish a line, then step back — and English readers who expect chapters to follow one another in time find a contradiction where the text intends an overlap.
  • v5 "separated out" — niphredu, and the same verb closes the chapter in v32. The word for what happens to the nations is separation, the neutral term you would use of branches dividing. Nothing here is a punishment yet.
  • v8 "He began" — hechel. This verb has been quietly marking the chapter turns: then it was begun to call on the name of the LORD (4:26), humankind began to be many (6:1), Noah began as a man of the ground (9:20), and now Nimrod begins to be a mighty one. Four beginnings, and the last two go badly.
  • v8, 9 "a mighty one… a mighty hunter" — gibbor, the same word as ha-gibborim in 6:4, the mighty ones born before the flood who were "the men of the name." The flood was supposed to have ended them. Four verses after the last genealogy, the word is back.
  • v9 "before the LORD" — lifnei YHWH, which ordinarily means in the presence of and carries no criticism at all. Every sinister reading of Nimrod — hunter of men, rebel, tyrant — comes from later tradition, not from these two verses. What the Hebrew says is that he was famous enough to become a proverb, and that his kingdom began at Babel.
  • v10 "Babel" — named here, in the land of Shinar, before chapter 11 gets to it. The reader is told whose city it is before being told what happened there.
